prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- More than 100 Romanians fled their homes Tuesday night in Belfast, Northern Ireland, following what politicians called "racist attacks and intimidation." A Romanian woman and her child are escorted by police in Belfast on Wednesday. "On Tuesday evening, when the Romanians saw their windows starting to be smashed, they felt the threats were very real and contacted the police," said Trish Morgan, the media relations manager at the Belfast City Church, which took them in. A church member was advised by the police that "the situation was getting too tense," and that the group -- 113 people in all -- needed to find a safe place that could accommodate them quickly. The member contacted the church, and that's where they went, Morgan said. The Romanians were "quite scared" upon arrival at the church but "relieved to be out of the situation," she added. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown Wednesday condemned what one member of Parliament called "appalling racist attacks," and said he hoped the authorities would be able to "take all the action necessary to protect them." Martin McGuinness, the deputy first minister of Northern Ireland -- a province of the United Kingdom -- visited the families on Wednesday, his party Sinn Fein announced. "People are shocked and completely disgusted by this incident," he said in a statement "I came here this morning to show very clearly my commitment to facing up to any form of intimidation in our community, no matter where it may come from. "I met with numerous families who are genuinely fearful for their lives and those of their families; I held a five-day-old baby girl in my arms today. She was born in Belfast and now forced to leave her home as a result of attacks by racist, criminal thugs," McGuinness said. He was speaking at the O-Zone leisure center, where the families have moved because the space is larger than the church. Race-hate crime in south Belfast has increased in the past six months, Sinn Fein equality and human rights expert Vincent Parker said. The incident came only a day after violence broke out at an anti-racism rally in support of Romanians in Belfast. Belfast Lord Mayor Naomi Long called Monday's scuffles "totally unacceptable." "A small minority of people have sadly taken away from an event which had been organized by the local community to show solidarity for their Romanian neighbors, and to express their abhorrence at their homes being subjected to racist attacks," she said Tuesday. CNN's Eve Bower contributed to this report.

**More Than 100 Romanians Flee Belfast After Racist Attacks and Intimidation**

**BELFAST, Northern Ireland —** More than 100 Romanian immigrants, including families with young children, have fled their homes in Belfast after a series of racist attacks and intimidation, officials and community leaders said, in an episode that has shocked Northern Ireland and drawn condemnation from across the political spectrum.

The group, many of them Roma families, left their homes in south Belfast after several nights of threats, smashed windows and hostile demonstrations outside their residences. Some initially took refuge in a local church before being moved to emergency accommodation as authorities assessed their safety.

Trish Morgan, a community worker who helped support the families, said the victims were terrified and felt they had no choice but to leave.

“They were frightened for their children and frightened for their lives,” Morgan said. “These are families who came here hoping for safety and a better future, and instead they were met with hatred.”

British Prime Minister Gordon Brown condemned the attacks, calling them unacceptable and insisting that racism had no place in the United Kingdom.

“This is completely unacceptable behavior,” Brown said. “People have a right to live free from intimidation, and those responsible for racist violence must be dealt with by the law.”

Northern Ireland Deputy First Minister Martin McGuinness also denounced the intimidation, saying the attacks had brought shame on Belfast.

“I am deeply ashamed that people who came here to live and work have been treated in this way,” McGuinness said. “There can be no excuse and no justification for racist attacks on vulnerable families.”

Police said they were investigating reports of intimidation and criminal damage. Authorities have faced questions over whether enough was done to protect the families before they fled.

Vincent Parker, speaking on behalf of local support organizations, said the incident exposed the fear faced by minority communities in parts of the city.

“This was not just a few broken windows,” Parker said. “It was a campaign of intimidation that made people believe they were not safe in their own homes.”

Naomi Long, a Belfast political leader, said the attacks did not represent the city as a whole and urged residents to stand against racism.

“Belfast must send a clear message that racist intimidation will not be tolerated,” Long said. “The people responsible are a small minority, but the damage they have done to these families and to the city’s reputation is enormous.”

The families’ departure comes at a sensitive time for Northern Ireland, which has worked for years to move beyond sectarian conflict and build a more inclusive society. Community leaders said the violence showed that racism remains a serious challenge, particularly for migrant and Roma communities.

Many of the Romanians were expected to leave Northern Ireland altogether, with some planning to return to Romania. Aid workers said the families were exhausted, frightened and uncertain about their future.

“This is a humanitarian situation,” Morgan said. “Whatever happens next, these people need dignity, safety and support.”

The families, many of them members of the Roma community, were targeted in attacks that included smashed windows, threats and verbal abuse. Police said they were treating the incidents as racially motivated.

**Sinn Féin** representatives were among those who denounced the violence, calling for solidarity with the Romanian families and urging authorities to ensure that racist attacks were not tolerated in any community. Instead, police had to intervene after disorder broke out, underscoring the volatility surrounding the issue and the depth of divisions exposed by the attacks.

For many of the Romanian families, the fear proved too great. Some chose to leave Northern Ireland altogether, returning to Romania despite having come to Belfast in search of work and a better life.

Community workers said the episode revealed both the vulnerability of migrant families and the importance of local support networks. Belfast City Church and the O-Zone leisure center became temporary symbols of refuge, but the attacks also raised difficult questions about whether authorities had done enough to protect minority communities.

The 2009 attacks remain one of Belfast’s most widely reported racist incidents, remembered not only for the intimidation that drove families from their homes, but also for the public reckoning that followed over racism, community responsibility and the safety of migrants in Northern Ireland.
